lesson.title: VLANs: One Switch, Many Logical Networks
lesson.summary: A VLAN, or virtual LAN, lets a single physical switch behave as if it were several completely separate networks, each with its own broadcast domain, without any extra cabling. It is the standard way modern networks solve the broadcast domain scaling problem raised in the previous chapter.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter ended on a real limitation: a switch, by itself, never shrinks a broadcast domain, no matter how many switches you chain together. Historically, the only way to keep one department's broadcast traffic away from another's was to buy each department its own physical switch and connect those switches only through a router. A VLAN, short for virtual LAN and standardized as part of IEEE 802.1Q, solves the same problem in software instead of hardware: it lets a single physical switch, or a group of switches, be logically carved into multiple independent broadcast domains, each behaving as if it were its own separate network, without a single extra cable.

The mechanism is conceptually simple. An administrator assigns each switch port to a VLAN, identified by a number, such as VLAN 10 for Sales or VLAN 20 for Engineering. From that point on, the switch treats each VLAN as its own isolated world for forwarding purposes: it only floods broadcast frames to ports within the same VLAN as the sender, and it only forwards learned unicast traffic within that same VLAN. A device plugged into a VLAN 10 port and a device plugged into a VLAN 20 port can be sitting in adjacent slots on the very same physical switch, sharing the same backplane, and still be completely unable to reach each other directly, exactly as if they were on two entirely separate switches with no link between them.

This buys two things that matter enormously in real networks. The first is isolation: a guest Wi-Fi network's traffic can share the same physical switches as the corporate network while remaining fully separated from it, which is both a security boundary and a broadcast domain boundary. The second is flexibility of grouping independent of physical location: a VLAN is not tied to a single switch or a single wiring closet, so the Engineering VLAN can include ports on a switch on the second floor and ports on a different switch on the fifth floor, letting the logical network layout match how people actually work rather than how cables happen to run through the building.

Consider a company with one twenty four port switch serving three departments that used to require three separate switches to stay properly isolated. The administrator assigns ports 1 through 8 to VLAN 10 for Sales, ports 9 through 16 to VLAN 20 for Engineering, and ports 17 through 24 to VLAN 30 for Guest Wi-Fi. When a Sales PC on port 2 sends a broadcast frame, say an ARP request, the switch floods it only to ports 1 through 8, the other VLAN 10 members. Ports 9 through 24 never see it at all, even though it is the same physical switch and the same electrical hardware handling all three groups. If someone in Sales genuinely needs to reach a server sitting in the Engineering VLAN, that traffic cannot cross directly; it has to pass through a device operating at a higher layer, a router or a Layer 3 capable switch, with an interface participating in both VLANs.

One question this raises is what happens when a VLAN needs to span more than one physical switch, connected by a single cable, carrying traffic for several VLANs at once. A plain Ethernet frame has no field that says which VLAN it belongs to, so switches need a way to mark that information as frames cross between them. That marking mechanism, and the special kind of switch port designed to carry it, are exactly what the next two chapters cover.
